There is a quiet magic in the first thirty minutes of the morning before the rest of the world wakes up. The house is still, save for the low, rhythmic hum of the refrigerator and the steady drip of water in the kitchen sink. Outside, the sky shifts from bruised violet to a soft, bruised peach as the sun inches its way over the horizon. In these moments, time feels suspended. 

We spend so much of our lives rushing—hurrying to finish a task, sprinting to catch a train, racing against deadlines that seem to multiply the moment we look away. But the dawn doesn’t rush. It unfolds with a deliberate, unhurried grace. 

Holding a warm mug of coffee, watching the steam curl into the cool air, I am reminded of how much we miss when we are always looking toward the next thing. Modern life encourages constant productivity, turning every hobby into a side hustle and every moment of rest into something that must be earned. Yet, the most profound parts of being human are wildly inefficient. They cannot be optimized or automated. They require lingering.

Today, I want to practice the art of lingering. Noticing the way light hits the dust motes in the hallway. Listening to the distant, lonely call of a morning bird. Allowing a thought to wander without needing it to arrive anywhere useful. There is a quiet rebellion in simply existing, untouched for just a little while by the relentless demands of the world.
